label: Exhaustion and Burnout
framing: Exhaustion is not a badge and it is not a sin, but it is a signal. Scripture gives the tired body something our age refuses it, a built-in stop, a rhythm of rest that says the world will keep turning without your hands on it.
cultural: The Sabbath was given to a people just freed from slavery, where rest was the first thing a slave was denied, and so a day of ceasing became a declaration that they were no longer owned. Our own age has rebuilt that bondage by choice, wearing busyness as proof of worth, and calls the resulting collapse a personal weakness rather than the predictable end of a life with no off switch.
historical: The rhythm of work and rest is written into the first page of Scripture, where even God rested on the seventh day. The desert monks ordered their days around prayer and labor and sleep, the Benedictines of the sixth century built a whole rule on balanced hours, and Eugene Peterson in our own time warned pastors that a busyness worn as a status symbol is a betrayal of the calling.
application: Guard a real day of ceasing each week, not a day of errands but a day that stops. Sleep as an act of trust, since the God who keeps Israel does not slumber and does not need you awake to run the world. Learn to say no, since every yes is a no to something, and ask whether your exhaustion is the cost of love or the cost of trying to be God.

verses.text: But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?”
verses.where: At the end of a long day of teaching by the lake, Jesus falls asleep in the stern of the boat on the cushion, and sleeps on through a storm. The site's note says his sleep comes not from flight from God, as Jonah's did, but from trust in him. The Son of God had a body that needed sleep, and he gave it what it needed.

verses.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.
verses.where: Hebrews tells weary believers that their high priest is able to sympathize with their weaknesses. The site's plain note says the weaknesses here are human frailties, not sins, and that Christ knows tiredness, hunger, grief, fear and pain from the inside. So the tired can come to God with confidence and find grace to help in their time of need.

verses.text: Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter. “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”
verses.where: In Gethsemane, on the worst night of his life, Jesus finds his closest friends asleep. The site's note says the saying about a willing spirit and weak flesh names the gap between good intention and actual strength that every disciple knows. Its plain note asks you to notice how gently he speaks to them: he names their weakness, and he does not stop loving them.

verses.text: Once again the Philistines waged war against Israel, and David and his servants went down and fought against the Philistines; but David became exhausted. Then Ishbi-benob, a descendant of Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who was bearing a new sword, resolved to kill David. But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, “You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished.”
verses.where: In one of four brief battle reports at the end of the chapter, the text says simply that David became exhausted, and a giant warrior resolved to kill him. Abishai came to his aid, and David's men swore that he must never again go out with them to battle. Even Israel's strongest king came to the end of his strength, and the people who loved him made him stop.

verses.text: As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down.
verses.where: While Israel fights Amalek, Moses holds up his hands on the hilltop, and when his hands grow heavy, Aaron and Hur sit him on a stone and hold them up, one on each side, until sunset. The site's plain note asks whose arms you could hold up this week, and whether you have let anyone hold up yours.

verses.text: But Jacob replied, “My lord knows that the children are frail, and I must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. If they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die. Please let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will continue on slowly, at a comfortable pace for the livestock and children, until I come to my lord at Seir.”
verses.where: Esau offers to travel with Jacob, and Jacob declines, pointing to the weakest members of his company: young children and animals nursing their young, who would die if driven hard for even a day. The site's note says that, whatever Jacob's motives, his principle is sound: the pace is set by the weakest member of the company, not the strongest. Scripture later pictures God leading his own flock this way.

verses.text: I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me.
verses.where: By its heading this psalm comes from the time David fled from his own son Absalom, with enemies multiplying and voices saying God would not save him. In the middle of it he lies down, sleeps and wakes again, because the LORD sustains him. The site's plain note says to name what you fear to God tonight, and then hand it over.

verses.text: He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber. Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
verses.where: A traveler looks to the hills for help and is told that his Protector will neither slumber nor sleep. The site's plain note offers the line to anyone who needs a keeper who never sleeps when they cannot. Because God does not sleep, his people can.

verses.text: A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice.
verses.where: God presents his Servant, who will bring justice to the nations quietly and gently, without breaking a bruised reed or snuffing out a smoldering wick. Matthew applies the song to Jesus (Matthew 12:18-21). A life burned down to its last flicker is not something he throws away.

verses.text: In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.
verses.where: Paul admits that believers are weak and do not know how they ought to pray, and says the Spirit himself intercedes for them with groans too deep for words. The site's note calls the verse a comfort to anyone who cannot find words to pray: weakness in prayer is expected. Its plain note asks what it would mean to bring God even a wordless sigh.

misread.taken: “They will run and not grow weary” is taken to mean that a believer with enough faith should never be worn out, so that exhaustion is heard as a sign of weak faith and the answer is to push on harder.
misread.says: The promise begins by saying that even youths grow tired and weary: tiredness is part of being human, not a failure of faith. The site's note says the chapter speaks to exiles who were worn out in a foreign land, that the strength here is exchanged, not generated, and that the sequence ends not in soaring but in the ordinary daily walk, where the strength to keep going is most needed. Nothing in it tells a tired person to ignore the body's limits; it tells them where strength comes from.
misread.text: Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall. But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.

whole: If your tiredness will not lift with rest, or has come with despair or thoughts of hurting yourself, see a doctor and tell someone you trust; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Some exhaustion has a plain cause: a newborn who wakes every two hours, a parent who needs care through the night, a second job, an illness, a long grief. Some has no single cause, only years of days without margin. Many people are ashamed of being tired, as if the body's limits were a moral failure, and they push on until the body decides for them.

Scripture treats the body's limits as part of being a creature, not a flaw to be overcome. Jesus slept in a boat in a storm. His friends could not stay awake in Gethsemane, and he named their weakness gently. Even David, the warrior king, became exhausted in battle and had to be rescued. Hebrews says Christ sympathizes with our weaknesses, and the site's note on that verse counts tiredness among them. What Scripture resists is not tiredness but a life that refuses every limit, the quiet belief that everything depends on our staying awake. The psalm says the Protector of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, which means you can.

So the wisdom here is humble and practical. Sleep, and treat it as trust rather than lost time, as David did when he lay down with enemies all around. Let others hold up your arms, as Aaron and Hur held up Moses', and ask for the help you would gladly give someone else. Set the pace by the weakest in your care, yourself included, as Jacob did with his children and his flocks. Lay down what can be laid down. When you are too tired to pray, the Spirit helps in our weakness, and a sigh brought to God is a prayer. And if the tiredness does not lift with rest, see a doctor: weariness of body and mind can be illness, and getting care is not a lack of faith.

The hope Scripture holds out is not a life without weariness but a God who is never weary and does not despise the weary. His Servant will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest, and in the prophet, strength is something received by those who wait, enough for the ordinary daily walk. The world will keep turning while you sleep. It always did.
deep.sit: What would change this week if you believed that God is awake while you sleep, and whose offer of help have you been refusing?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says this psalm does not tell you to stop working; it says that worry is not the same as work, and that sleep is a gift. Pray it before you lie down tonight.
prayer.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat— for He gives sleep to His beloved.

careLines.text: If you are exhausted and it does not lift, or if weariness has turned into despair, please see a doctor or talk to a pastor or a crisis line.
Weariness of body and mind can be illness, and getting care is not a lack of faith.
If sleepless nights have become your normal, please tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
